title: Game server outage windows
prompt:
A monitoring bot pings each game server and stores one row per check with a check_no that increases over time. When the bot is restarted some check numbers are skipped, so the numbers are not contiguous.

An outage is a maximal run of failed checks (is_up = false) for one server with no successful check between them. Skipped numbers do not end an outage.

Return one row per outage.

- Columns: server_id, first_check, last_check, failed_checks
- Any row order is fine
- failed_checks is the number of failed rows in the outage
- Servers that never failed return no rows
hints: Grouping all failed checks per server merges separate outages. You need a label that changes whenever an up check interrupts.
check_no minus row_number() breaks on skipped numbers. Instead, compare two row numbers: one over all of a server's checks and one over its checks with the same is_up value.

row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY server_id ORDER BY check_no) - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY server_id, is_up ORDER BY check_no) is constant within a run. Keep NOT is_up and group by server_id and that difference.

exercise.starter:
-- One row per outage
SELECT server_id,
       min(check_no) AS first_check,
       max(check_no) AS last_check,
       count(*) AS failed_checks
FROM health_checks
WHERE NOT is_up
GROUP BY server_id;
exercise.solution:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT server_id, check_no, is_up,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY server_id ORDER BY check_no)
       - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY server_id, is_up ORDER BY check_no) AS grp
  FROM health_checks
)
SELECT server_id,
       min(check_no) AS first_check,
       max(check_no) AS last_check,
       count(*) AS failed_checks
FROM x
WHERE NOT is_up
GROUP BY server_id, grp;

explanation: Rows in the same run of equal is_up values advance both row numbers together, so their difference stays constant; any row with the other status advances only the overall counter and shifts the difference. Grouping failed rows by (server_id, difference) therefore yields exactly one group per outage. The trap is using check_no - row_number(): it only works when numbers are contiguous, and a skipped number would wrongly split one outage in two. Grouping all failed checks per server is the other common mistake, merging separate outages into one.
notes: Both windows sort on different keys, so Postgres usually runs two sorts; the primary key covers only the first. Note the difference value can repeat between an up-run and a down-run, which is why the filter on is_up (or grouping by it) is required. A lag()-based 'status changed' flag plus a running sum is an equivalent formulation and is easier to extend with extra break rules.
followUps: Also treat a gap of more than 5 skipped check numbers as the end of an outage.
Return only outages of 3 or more failed checks, and the longest outage per server.
